title: Story: the presentation tool I wanted between Figma and PowerPoint
summary: I needed the best of Figma and PPT, so I built Story: a browser-based presentation design environment with one source for design and delivery.

body.markdown: I needed the best of Figma and PPT, so I created **Story**. Figma has the canvas, precision and reusable design-system thinking I want when I am shaping ideas visually. PowerPoint has the slide structure, presenter workflow and output muscle that real presentations still depend on. I did not want to keep choosing which half of the job mattered more.

Story is my attempt to make those two instincts live in one browser-based environment: a place where the authored deck remains the source of truth from design, through rehearsal, to delivery and export.

body.text: The gap I wanted to close

body.markdown: Design tools are excellent at craft: direct manipulation, precise objects, styles, variables, components and collaborative editing. Presentation tools are excellent at the ceremony of a talk: slides, masters, layouts, notes, transitions, presenter view, export and printing. The trouble starts when a high-stakes story needs both.

The Story specification says parity with Figma and PowerPoint is the adoption floor, not the reason to choose it. The reason is the governed bridge: one living presentation system that can produce audience editions, deterministic live runs and professional outputs without duplicate-deck drift or silent fidelity loss.

body.text: A design editor that knows it has to present

body.markdown: I started from the parts of authoring that make a tool feel serious: a visual editor, slide management, master slides and layouts, a rich property inspector, layers, presentation mode, speaker notes, presenter workflows and cloud storage foundations. The README describes those as Story's current foundations, not as a finished claim.

That is why even a small inspector detail matters. Fills, strokes and effects are not just formatting rows; they are layered systems that need to survive editing, reuse and output. A presentation tool can hide that complexity. A presentation design environment has to make it understandable.

body.text: The product promise is one source

body.markdown: The direction of Story is intentionally bigger than drawing better slides. The product spec frames it as a professional environment where teams design with Figma-class control, author and deliver with PowerPoint-class completeness, and maintain the result as one governed narrative system.

That means the same document model should feed the editor, thumbnails, presentation runtime, presenter view, export, print and collaboration. If a feature exists in only one surface, or silently degrades somewhere else, it is not really complete.

The repo is honest about its current state. The capability audit calls Story a capable design-first slide editor, with strong foundations in direct manipulation, shape primitives, booleans and masks, layered styling, master/layout inheritance, transitions, notes and baseline presentation runtime.

It is also honest about what remains: shared document architecture, deeper Figma-class layout and components, PowerPoint-class charts and recording, PPTX interoperability, autosave, recovery, multiplayer collaboration, accessibility and performance gates. I like that discipline. It keeps the project from mistaking a control for a product.

You can see the code on [GitHub](https://github.com/prabinpebam/story) and read its documentation at [prabinpebam.github.io/story](https://prabinpebam.github.io/story/). Story is still a side project, but it is the kind I enjoy most: a product question made concrete enough to touch, test and keep refining.
